Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

acute dystonia · akathisia · parkinsonism · tardive dyskinesia · neuroleptic malignant syndrome · metabolic and prolactin effectsWhich effect, timed from the start or the last dose increase, and what is the next step?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Drug script
Bottom line
  • Clock it from the start or last increase: dystonia hours to days, akathisia and parkinsonism weeks, tardive dyskinesia months to years
  • Fever lead-pipe rigidity confusion building over days neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): stop the drug, then cool and give fluids
  • Clozapine ANC (absolute neutrophil count) before and during; clozapine and olanzapine most metabolic harm; screen everyone at least yearly
What it is

Dopamine receptor blockers: antipsychotics antiemetics such as metoclopramide and prochlorperazine

Mechanism

Blockade in the striatum acetylcholine outweighs dopamine dystonia and parkinsonism

Anticholinergic balance restored dystonia usually eases within minutes

Used for

Psychosis: second-generation drugs favored first line

Schizophrenia after 2 or more failed adequate trials clozapine

Acute mania severe agitation in delirium

Risks

NMS laryngeal dystonia clozapine: severe neutropenia, myocarditis, seizures

Movement: dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia

Metabolic (clozapine, olanzapine) prolactin (first-generation, risperidone) QTc (haloperidol)

Insights

Every class can cause NMS, second generation included switching drugs is no safeguard

Anticholinergics relieve dystonia and parkinsonism, but may worsen tardive dyskinesia, so stop them there

Adverse effects, by time coursedetail behind the risks
HoursAcute dystonia, usually within hours of the first dose; an emergency department antiemetic can do itlaryngeal spasm can stop breathing
DaysNMS builds over 1 to 3 days, usually after a start or dose increase (the main risk factor) but possible at any timerisk highest with high-potency or depot drugs, several antipsychotics together, or added lithium
WeeksAkathisia, the most common extrapyramidal effect, typically within 4 weeks; parkinsonism within days to weeks, tremor often on both sides
Months to yearsTardive dyskinesia after prolonged use, more than 6 months; about 10% to 20% after a year of treatmentorofacial forms are commonest
After stoppingWithdrawal-emergent dyskinesia after an abrupt stop, more common in children; clears in 4 to 12 weeks
ClozapineAgranulocytosis in just under 1%, usually within 3 months; the risk never reaches zero
By potencyHigh-potency first-generation drugs (eg haloperidol), more so at higher doses, drive extrapyramidal effects; low-potency drugs and clozapine are the most anticholinergic and sedatingseizures too are commonest with low-potency drugs and clozapine, especially at high doses
Who is at riskHigher-potency drugs, higher doses, prior extrapyramidal effects; young men for dystonia, older women for parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia
2Urgent risks
NMSFever, rigidity, confusion and unstable vital signs on a dopamine blocker
CK (creatine kinase) can be very high and typically tracks severity Labs: leukocytosis, myoglobin in the urine, falling kidney function Most often high-potency first-generation (eg haloperidol), but any class, olanzapine included

If NMS is suspected, choose stopping the antipsychotic, then cooling and fluids.

AirwayDystonia of the larynx or pharynx

If breathing is threatened, choose airway assessment and an intravenous anticholinergic.

ClozapineSevere neutropenia; also myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, seizures, profound hypotension
ANC before starting and throughout treatment Agranulocytosis usually within 3 months

If the baseline ANC is under 1500/µL, choose not starting clozapine (initiation is not recommended).

DementiaOlder adults with dementia-related psychosis
Boxed warning, first- and second-generation alike: death risk about 1.6 to 1.7 times higher
3Differential
Which effect is it, most tempting first
EffectFingerprintDecides it
Acute dystoniaSustained, painful spasm of neck, jaw, eyes or tongue; mind clear; antiemetics such as metoclopramide can cause itWithin hours to days of a start or increase; half by 48 hours, 90% by day 5
AkathisiaInner restlessness, a driven urge to move; pacesTypically within 4 weeks of a start or increase; the restlessness is felt from within
Drug-induced parkinsonismTremor, rigidity, slow movement, masked face, shuffling gaitDays to a few weeks; tremor often symmetric; reversible
Tardive dyskinesiaLip smacking, tongue darting, cheek puffing, jaw movementsMonths to years of treatment, usually past 6 months
Neuroleptic malignant syndromeFever, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability, high CKUsually after a start or increase (the main risk factor), but possible at any time; builds over 1 to 3 days; no clonus
HypocalcemiaFacial muscle spasmParesthesia, hyperreflexia and a cause such as neck surgery
Fever, agitation, clonus, hyperreflexia, vomiting or diarrheaWithin hours (under 24) of a serotonergic change; clonus, not rigidity
Malignant hyperthermiaFever and rigidity, as in NMSDuring or just after a volatile anesthetic or succinylcholine
CatatoniaLittle movement, unresponsive, posturingPlain catatonia does not explain fever or autonomic instability; the malignant form can, but shows posturing and waxy flexibility
Angioedema or anaphylaxisTongue pushed outSwelling, not spasm
Withdrawal-emergent dyskinesiaNew dyskinesia, often in a childAfter an abrupt stop; clears in 4 to 12 weeks
Galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction, bone lossAny first-generation drug or risperidone

Pause point. The bait: NMS offered as serotonin syndrome from a drug interaction, or as malignant hyperthermia, and dystonia offered as hypocalcemia or as agitation needing more haloperidol. Rigidity and fever building over days on a dopamine blocker is NMS; a spasm within hours in an alert patient is dystonia, and an anticholinergic treats it.

7Treatment
Manage by effect
EffectDoAvoid
Acute dystoniaA parenteral anticholinergic (benztropine or diphenhydramine); relief usually within 10 to 30 minutes; intravenous benztropine is followed by an oral doseMore haloperidol: further blockade would likely worsen it
AkathisiaLower the dose or switch (clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine); propranolol if the dose must stayReaching first for a benzodiazepine or benztropine (less favorable safety)
ParkinsonismLower the dose or switch to a second-generation drug; amantadine, or an anticholinergic short termAnticholinergics in older adults
Tardive dyskinesiaStop anticholinergics; valbenazine or deutetrabenazine if moderate to severe; stop the antipsychotic or switch (eg clozapine) if possibleAnticholinergics: they may worsen it
Neuroleptic malignant syndromeStop the antipsychotic, then cool and correct fluids and electrolytes (ladder below)Swapping in another antipsychotic: every class can cause it
Metabolic harmSwitch to a lower-risk drug such as aripiprazole (lowest tier: aripiprazole, risperidone, ziprasidone, high-potency first-generation drugs)Clozapine and olanzapine carry the most
Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementiaQuetiapine, pimavanserin or clozapineRisperidone, olanzapine, typical drugs; in Lewy body dementia typical drugs, even at very low doses, tend to worsen extrapyramidal signs
High-risk patient (eg young man, prior dystonia) given an intramuscular first-generation drugGive diphenhydramine or benztropine with it
1

FirstNMS suspected

Stop the antipsychotic
2

Supportivethen, once it is stopped

Aggressive cooling; correct volume deficits and electrolytes

Admit to an intensive care unit for close monitoring; a benzodiazepine may help agitation. Case reportsElectroconvulsive therapy (ECT) has been reported to work in refractory cases.

3

Optionsbeyond supportive care

Bromocriptine (a dopamine agonist) or dantrolene (a muscle relaxant)
8Follow-up
Monitoring
WhenCheckWhy
Every patientMetabolic screening at least yearly, with counseling against weight gainClozapine and olanzapine carry the most metabolic risk
Second-generation drug, from the startWeight at baseline, 4, 8 and 12 weeks, then quarterly; glucose and blood pressure at baseline, 12 weeks, then yearly; lipids at baseline, 12 weeks, then every 5 yearsSchedule adapted from the 2004 American Diabetes Association consensus
On clozapineANC before starting, weekly to month 6, every 2 weeks to month 12, then monthlySevere neutropenia, likeliest early, never zero
Starting haloperidol (eg, for delirium)Baseline ECG (electrocardiogram) for the QTc (rate-corrected QT interval)QTc prolongation; most marked with thioridazine and ziprasidone
Long-term useOrofacial movementsAbout 10% to 20% develop tardive dyskinesia after a year of treatment
Restarting after NMSWait at least 2 weeks after it resolves; a lower-potency drug, low dose, slow titrationThe recommended cautious rechallenge
Missed periods or nipple dischargeWhether the patient takes a prolactin-raising drug (any first-generation drug, risperidone) Prolactin rises
Practice
  1. 23-year-old man given intramuscular haloperidol for agitation 8 hours ago now his neck is twisted to the right and his eyes are fixed upward Alert; speaks clearly; no stridor T 37.1 °C · HR 104/min · BP 138/84 mm Hg → Benztropine → acute dystonia within hours of a dopamine blocker: an anticholinergic such as benztropine gives rapid relief; dantrolene belongs to neuroleptic malignant syndrome and propranolol to akathisia
  2. 19-year-old woman in the emergency department for vomiting 1 hour after intravenous metoclopramide: jaw clenched, tongue pushing out, words slurred Fully alert; no lip or tongue swelling; no wheeze BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 96/min → Diphenhydramine → an antiemetic dopamine blocker caused acute dystonia: a parenteral anticholinergic such as diphenhydramine usually works within 30 minutes; dantrolene belongs to neuroleptic malignant syndrome and propranolol to akathisia
  3. 34-year-old man started haloperidol 2 weeks ago for schizophrenia cannot sit through visits; paces, shifts his legs, says he feels driven to move voices quieter; dose cannot be lowered HR 82/min · no rigidity or tremor → Add propranolol → inner restlessness with a compelling urge to move within 4 weeks of starting is akathisia; propranolol treats it when the dose cannot be lowered; more haloperidol would worsen it, and valbenazine is for tardive dyskinesia
  4. 46-year-old woman whose risperidone dose was doubled 3 weeks ago both hands shake at rest; slower walking with short steps; blank face No lip smacking or tongue movements T 36.9 °C · cogwheel rigidity both arms · alert, oriented → Drug-induced parkinsonism → tremor, rigidity, slow shuffling gait and masked face within weeks of a dose increase; tardive dyskinesia comes months to years later with orofacial movements, and there is no fever or altered mental status
  5. 58-year-old man with schizophrenia on haloperidol for 9 years constant lip smacking and tongue darting that embarrass him and disrupt eating takes benztropine as well BP 128/80 mm Hg · no tremor or rigidity → Stop benztropine and start valbenazine → orofacial movements after years of a dopamine blocker are tardive dyskinesia; anticholinergics may worsen it and should be stopped, and moderate to severe disease is treated with a VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter 2) inhibitor
  6. 52-year-old man started on risperidone for schizophrenia 6 days ago now disoriented, diaphoretic and rigid in all limbs T 40.3 °C · BP 172/100 mm Hg · HR 118/min · reflexes normal, no clonus · creatine kinase 24,000 U/L → Neuroleptic malignant syndrome → fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability and a high CK developing over days, even from a second-generation drug; serotonin syndrome comes within hours with clonus and hyperreflexia; acute dystonia is a localized spasm of the neck, jaw, eyes or tongue
  7. 29-year-old woman started on haloperidol in hospital 4 days ago rigid, confused, febrile; creatine kinase rising No new serotonergic drugs T 39.8 °C · HR 120/min · BP 164/98 mm Hg · urine dark → Stop haloperidol; cool; give fluids → neuroleptic malignant syndrome: stopping the drug is paramount, then aggressive cooling and fluids; another antipsychotic can cause it too, an anticholinergic does not treat it, and bromocriptine or dantrolene are options beyond supportive care
  8. 32-year-old man with schizophrenia stable on olanzapine for 1 year gained 14 kg; new fasting glucose 128 mg/dL Wants to stay on an antipsychotic BMI (body mass index) 33 kg/m² · BP 136/86 mm Hg · triglycerides 260 mg/dL → Aripiprazole → metabolic disturbances are greatest with clozapine and olanzapine, intermediate with quetiapine and lowest with aripiprazole; screen at least yearly
  9. 27-year-old woman with schizophrenia on risperidone for 8 months no periods for 4 months; milky nipple discharge Urine pregnancy test negative; no headaches TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) normal · BP 110/70 mm Hg · visual fields full → Dopamine blockade raising prolactin → risperidone, like any first-generation drug, commonly raises prolactin, causing amenorrhea and galactorrhea; a normal TSH argues against hypothyroidism, and risperidone commonly raises prolactin, so the drug is the likely cause
Pairs with SSRI Adverse Effects: hours after a serotonergic change, with clonus? Schizophrenia: Long-Term Care: monitoring the maintenance drug, with yearly metabolic screening?
Transferable rule

Time the movement from the start or the last dose increase before naming it: hours to days is dystonia, weeks is akathisia or parkinsonism, months to years is tardive dyskinesia.
